name: Whole-screen stimuli with only targeted knobs varied
source: D-optimal / Bayesian adaptive DCE design (idefix); live demo already does this
claim: Render complete realistic screens but vary only the knobs the round targets, holding others at the posterior mean.
limitations: Assumes posterior mean is a sensible hold value early on.

name: Content held constant across a comparison
claim: Use the same headline/copy/imagery in all cards of a round so content preference cannot confound the token-pack signal.
limitations: Some knobs (density) interact with content length.

name: P05 corpus components as re-themable controlled stimuli
source: research/21st-corpus-audit-2026-08-27.md — 86.7% of colour-bearing CSS rules already resolve through var(--token); 87.3% carry a shadcn oklch :root block
claim: Use the 8,515-identity corpus as the stimulus pool: identical structure, varying token pack, re-theming is a find-and-replace on ~30 custom properties.
limitations: 271 components lack previews; component SOURCE is absent from the corpus.

name: Stimulus realism gradient: abstract swatches -> component -> full screen
claim: Early rounds use cheap abstract stimuli, later rounds full screens.
limitations: Risks measuring preference for the abstraction, not the design.

name: Never re-show an identical stimulus
claim: Prevents familiarity inflating preference for repeated designs.
limitations: Constrains the generator's search near convergence.

name: Log stimulus-repetition rate as a measured confound
claim: Even if repeats occur, make the exposure effect measurable rather than invisible.

name: Industry-conditioned stimulus priors
claim: Seed the stimulus space from an industry prior (a law firm starts in a more conservative region than a course creator).
limitations: Risks stereotyping; must remain a prior, not a constraint.

name: Brand-constraint hard cutoffs before elicitation
claim: Existing brand colours/fonts become hard prunes of the stimulus space, not soft preferences; all later stimuli satisfy them.
limitations: Over-pruning can empty the space; needs a fallback.

name: Dark-mode variant shown as part of the stimulus
claim: Show each candidate in both modes since packs must ship both.
limitations: Doubles visual load per card.

name: Density stress-test stimuli using realistic long copy
claim: Include a card rendered with realistically long client copy so density preference is measured under real conditions.

name: Fragment rounds reserved for fine disambiguation only
claim: Use component fragments only when two knobs remain confounded at whole-screen scale.
limitations: Unproven that fragments resolve better.

name: Adaptive grid size by viewport
source: Sequential Gallery reduced 5x5 to 3x3 on a 13-inch display
claim: Gallery size should adapt to display, not be a fixed product constant.

name: Stimuli drawn from the closed pack catalogue only
claim: Never show a card that is not a real, gate-passing pack — so the preview IS the deliverable.
limitations: Restricts early exploration to catalogue coverage.

name: Preview must be re-rendered from spec, never the original thumbnail
claim: Closes the expectation gap by construction and makes previews a free end-to-end pipeline test.
limitations: Requires the render pipeline before elicitation ships.

name: Anti-prototypicality probe
source: Tuch et al. 2012; Reber et al. 2004
claim: Deliberately include one low-prototypicality card per round to detect clients who want distinctive over safe.
limitations: May be systematically rejected, wasting a slot.

name: Seed from client's existing website via extraction
source: Canva AI extracts brand context from a public URL
claim: Warm-start the prior from the client's current site rather than a uniform prior.
limitations: Their current site may be exactly what they want to escape.

name: Competitor-anchored stimuli
claim: Show packs near and far from named competitors to elicit differentiation preference.
limitations: Conflates taste with positioning.

name: Stimulus set diversity floor
source: Negahban et al. spectral gap dependence
claim: Enforce a minimum pairwise distance among the 4 cards so the comparison graph stays well-connected.
limitations: Competes with least-resolved-knob targeting, which wants NEAR pairs.

name: 4-up gallery with explicit outside option
source: derived §3 + Sawtooth 4-5 per screen + live demo
claim: 2.32 noiseless bits/round; ~0.91 effective at p=0.15; balances information against deliberation cost and avoids the hostility of 'worst'.
limitations: Best-worst is strictly more informative per question.

name: Best-worst of 4 (MaxDiff Case 1)
claim: 3.58 noiseless bits/round, ~2x the 4-up rate; would cut rounds to ~3.
limitations: Roughly doubles per-screen deliberation; 'pick the worst' is hostile in a client sales context; no verified numeric information-gain multiplier exists.
disposition: test as an A/B arm — falsifier F6

name: Attribute-level best-worst (MaxDiff Case 2)
claim: 'Which knob is most and least right on THIS design' — maps almost exactly onto per-knob credit assignment, solving the attribution problem a whole-card pick has.
limitations: Requires the client to reason about knobs explicitly, which is exactly what we said they cannot do.

name: Binary pairwise
claim: Simplest, but ~11 rounds at p=0.15 and most sensitive to near-ties.
limitations: Nearly double the rounds of 4-up.

name: Three-way pairwise with a neutral middle
source: Midjourney legacy Style Tuner: 'leave the middle box selected to skip the pair'
claim: A shipped outside-option affordance inside a pairwise format.
limitations: Fewer bits than 4-up.
disposition: reference — the affordance, not the format

name: Full ranking of 4
claim: 4.58 noiseless bits, the densest format tested.
limitations: Ranking four whole screens is a heavy cognitive task; inherits IIA.

name: 9-up gallery
claim: 3.17 noiseless bits.
limitations: Nine whole-screen renders exceed comfortable simultaneous comparison; selection noise rises in a way the bit count does not capture.

name: Mixed format by phase: 4-up early, pairwise late
claim: Broad exploration wants breadth; fine disambiguation is naturally pairwise.
limitations: Format switching may confuse users and complicates the likelihood.

name: Slider direct manipulation as a fallback
claim: Offer sliders to clients who DO know what they want, skipping elicitation entirely.
limitations: Most clients cannot name a radius; the slider is the competitor's approach.

name: Sequential line search (1D slider through knob space)
source: Koyama et al. SIGGRAPH 2017 (MIT-licensed implementation exists)
claim: User picks a point on a 1D slice; reported 15-iteration budget, good by iteration 4-5 at 6D/7D.
limitations: A slider over a design continuum is harder to render than 4 discrete packs, and our output space is discrete anyway.

name: Outside option as weak negative evidence on all shown cards
source: derived; diverges from Midjourney which makes skipping non-informative
claim: Preserves information from declines while keeping the re-roll honest.
limitations: Weight is a free parameter needing calibration.

name: Cap consecutive outside-option selections at 3
claim: Three declines in a row means the generator is in the wrong region; trigger a re-seed rather than another round.
limitations: Threshold is arbitrary pending data.

name: 'This is right' always-available terminal affordance
source: Sequential Gallery satisfaction button; mean 5.36 rounds to satisfaction
claim: User's own judgement is the criterion the whole exercise proxies for.
limitations: Users may satisfice early.

name: Preview-before-commit on the selected pack
claim: Let the client see the pack applied to their real content before committing.
limitations: Requires the render pipeline.

name: Paired-comparison tie option distinct from 'none'
claim: 'These two are equally good' is different information from 'both are wrong'.
limitations: Adds a third response category to model.

name: Confidence-weighted responses (client marks how sure they are)
claim: Let the client flag a low-confidence pick so it is down-weighted.
limitations: Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated; adds friction.

name: BALD acquisition on a GP preference model
claim: Information gain expressed via predictive entropies, explicitly extended to GP preference learning; tractable.
limitations: Myopic one-step criterion.

name: qEUBO acquisition
source: Astudillo et al. AISTATS 2023; shipped in BoTorch
claim: One-step Bayes optimal under noise-free responses; simple regret converges at o(1/n); qEI can FAIL to converge for PBO.
limitations: Asymptotic guarantee gives no finite-sample count.

name: Target the least-resolved knob each round
claim: Constructs cards differing on the widest-posterior axis while holding others steady.
limitations: Greedy per-knob targeting can miss interaction effects.

name: Explicit exploration/exploitation schedule ('candy vs medicine')
claim: Deliberately mix near-certain-hit cards (engagement) with high-information cards (learning).
limitations: Ratio unpublished; costs information per round.

name: Hierarchical Bayes shrinkage toward a population prior
claim: Designed exactly for the few-observations-per-individual regime; the primary anti-overfitting mechanism alongside closed packs.
limitations: Needs a population of prior clients to shrink toward.
disposition: ADOPT — but cold-start it from I40

name: Warm-start prior from a population aesthetic model
source: LAION aesthetic predictor; Brochu et al. 2010 cut iterations 11.25 -> 6.5 with a learned prior
claim: Learn the client's DEVIATION from a population baseline rather than their taste from scratch. The largest single efficiency lever reported anywhere in the applied literature.
limitations: Population aesthetic is not per-client taste and may encode a generic bias.

name: D-optimal / Bayesian-efficient stimulus set selection
claim: Choose the 4 cards to maximise design efficiency under the current posterior.
limitations: GPL-3 licence; requires priors.

name: Simulate-to-size: Monte Carlo power analysis for round count
claim: Answer 'how many rounds' EMPIRICALLY by simulating synthetic clients under a BT likelihood rather than arguing from bounds.
limitations: Power analysis is built for GLM responses; needs adapting.
disposition: ADOPT — this is how the N question should actually be settled

name: Orthogonal-array fixed design as the passive baseline
claim: The non-adaptive control our adaptive policy must beat.

name: Projective preferential BO for high-dim knob spaces
claim: Queries along projections, designed for human-in-the-loop high-dimensional elicitation.
limitations: Small research repo (20 stars).

name: Transitivity-based pair elimination (PAPRIKA-style)
source: 1000minds method; COULD NOT VERIFY — 404 on both URLs
claim: Eliminate implied comparisons by transitivity, drastically cutting explicit questions.
limitations: SOURCE UNVERIFIED. Also assumes transitivity, which human taste violates (Ailon 2010).

name: Non-transitivity-tolerant active ranking
claim: Explicitly handles 'non-transitivity paradoxes which may arise naturally due to human mistakes or irrationality'.
limitations: No closed-form bound extracted from the abstract.

name: Copeland counting as a simplicity check
claim: Rank by comparisons won: optimal up to CONSTANT factors, no conditions on the probability matrix. If this matches the GP model's output, the GP is not earning its complexity.
limitations: Top-k recovery framing, not utility-vector recovery.

name: Dueling-bandit formulation
source: Yue & Joachims; Zoghi RUCB; Sui et al. survey
claim: Relative-feedback online optimisation.
limitations: Regret-minimisation over continuous operation, not fixed-budget identification — a different objective from ours.

name: Per-knob independent BT models vs joint GP
claim: Independent per-knob models are simpler and interpretable; a joint GP captures correlation.
limitations: Independence is empirically false (§4 of first-principles).

name: Bootstrap confidence intervals over pairwise judgments
claim: Battle-tested approach to reporting uncertainty on BT fits from human votes.

name: TrueSkill-style Gaussian belief per pack
source: Herbrich et al. 2007; use openskill.py (MIT), NOT sublee/trueskill
claim: Calibrated per-item uncertainty that Elo does not give.
limitations: LICENCE TRAP: sublee/trueskill's LICENSE body bars commercial use despite a BSD badge.

name: Stop when expected information gain of the best next question < threshold
claim: A wide posterior no available question can narrow is a reason to stop, not to continue.
limitations: Threshold (~0.25 bits) needs calibration.

name: Three-condition stop: confidence OR ceiling OR user-satisfied
source: derived §6; Brochu 2010 20-iteration abandonment; Midjourney 'past round 15... small and subtle'
claim: Primary rule is confidence; 15 rounds is a ceiling; user satisfaction always terminates.
limitations: Ceiling is grounded in two sources, not a derivation.

name: Hard floor of 5 rounds
claim: Early apparent convergence is usually the prior, not the data.

name: Per-knob confidence reporting, never a single scalar
claim: Some knobs resolve in two rounds; others may never resolve, and 'this client does not care about shadow' is a finding not a failure. A single '87% confident' number would mislead.
limitations: More complex to present to a non-technical client.

name: 'No preference' as a first-class per-knob outcome
claim: Explicitly represent indifference rather than forcing a point estimate.
limitations: Downstream pack selection must handle a free knob.

name: Two-week test-retest stability as the primary validation metric
claim: A model that fits the clicks but changes answer next Tuesday is worthless. Measures whether the thing we claim to measure exists.
limitations: Requires client time two weeks apart; hard to get.

name: Held-out pick prediction as the fit metric
claim: Reserve 2 rounds, predict them from the model fitted on the rest.
limitations: Small n makes the estimate noisy.

name: Neighbour-discrimination test
claim: Show the client their pack plus the 2nd and 3rd nearest, unlabelled. If they cannot pick their own above chance, the catalogue is denser than perception.

name: Perturbation-tolerance test
claim: Show the converged pack and a +/-1-level perturbation. If clients reliably distinguish and reject, the tolerance argument in §2 collapses and round counts triple.

name: Separation-aware stopping
source: Chen & Suh 2015 — complexity scales inversely with separation
claim: Detect when remaining candidates are genuinely near-tied and stop rather than burning rounds distinguishing the indistinguishable.

name: Comparison-graph connectivity check
claim: BT/MM fitting requires a strongly connected comparison graph; verify before fitting.
limitations: Constrains which stimulus sets are legal.

name: Abandonment-rate monitoring as a UX stop signal
source: Brochu et al. 2010: 20 iterations is 'roughly the point at which users start to quit'
claim: Instrument drop-off per round; if it rises before the ceiling, lower the ceiling.

name: Time-per-round budget
claim: Budget total elicitation time, not just round count. 10 rounds x ~15s is ~2.5 minutes.
limitations: Whole-screen comparison likely slower than the cited subtask.

name: Confidence decay over calendar time
claim: Treat the profile as decaying, prompting re-elicitation rather than assuming permanence.
limitations: Decay rate unknown; needs I57 data first.

name: Re-elicitation triggered by client rejection of built output
claim: If a client rejects the delivered design, that is strong evidence to re-run rather than patch.
limitations: Expensive and reads as failure.

name: Continuous preference vector internally, closed pack at the boundary
source: derived §8; token-pack-science gates A-J; lane synthesis 'learn a vector not a pack ID'
claim: Catalogue can grow without re-eliciting; shipped artefact is always gate-passing.
limitations: Nearest-neighbour metric weighting is an open parameter.

name: Reject continuous token interpolation
source: token-pack-science §5 Gate C — WCAG luminance is non-linear in channel values
claim: The midpoint of two AA-passing palettes can fail AA; an interpolated pack has passed none of gates A-J.
limitations: Loses expressive range between packs.

name: Closed-pack snapping AS the anti-overfitting regularizer
claim: Output space of ~20-30 packs rather than 36,000 means the model cannot overfit into a bespoke corner on ten noisy clicks.
limitations: If the catalogue grows large this protection weakens.

name: Explain the pack choice in knob terms
claim: 'We chose this because you are here in knob space' is worth real money in the client conversation.
limitations: Requires knob names clients understand.

name: Weighted knob-space distance metric
claim: Typography and chroma likely dominate perception; equal weighting is probably wrong.
limitations: Weights must be fitted, adding parameters.

name: Second- and third-choice packs offered alongside the first
claim: Offering the top 3 both hedges model error and generates validation data for free.
limitations: Reintroduces choice at the moment we claimed to have decided.

name: TasteProfile schema: per-knob posterior mean + interval + n_observations
claim: Makes uncertainty first-class and auditable in the output contract.

name: PreferenceConfidence as a per-knob vector, not a scalar
claim: Mirrors I55 in the output contract.

name: DesignDNA as a versioned, reproducible artefact
claim: Pin the model version, catalogue version, and elicitation transcript so a profile is reproducible.

name: Preference vector pre-filters P05 component suggestions
claim: The same vector that picks a pack can rank components, so elicitation pays for itself twice.
limitations: Component preference may not be the same construct as pack preference.

name: Preference vector seeds image-generation rounds
claim: Reuse for generated imagery.
limitations: Unverified that the vector transfers to a different modality.

name: Per-context confidence (marketing page vs dense dashboard)
claim: A client's density preference on a landing page may differ from a dashboard. Model context as a conditioning variable rather than assuming one profile fits all surfaces.
limitations: Multiplies the parameter count by the number of contexts, directly worsening the sample-size problem.
disposition: test — this is the open question with the worst cost/benefit

name: Single profile with per-context OFFSETS rather than separate profiles
claim: A cheaper resolution of I78: one taste vector plus small learned context deltas.
limitations: Offsets still need data to fit.

name: Stated vs revealed preference agreement metric
source: Pinterest deprecated onboarding interests in favour of engagement clusters
claim: Measure whether what the client PICKS matches what they later APPROVE in delivered work. The single most commercially important validation.
limitations: Requires delivered projects, so it is a slow metric.

name: Fall back to a safe default pack on low confidence
source: Shopify SDUI unknown-layout fallback; Netflix popular-set fallback
claim: If confidence is too low, ship an industry-appropriate default rather than a badly-inferred pack.

name: Log spec/pack collisions as a coverage signal
claim: If two different clients converge to identical packs, that tells you which knob to add.

name: Human review gate before pack is committed to a build
claim: A designer confirms the selected pack before it drives a client deliverable.
limitations: Costs human time per client; undermines the automation claim.

name: Profile portability across a client's multiple projects
claim: Reuse the DesignDNA for the same client's later work.
limitations: Preference may be project-specific, not client-specific.

name: Explicit re-elicitation rather than silent drift tracking
claim: Both major platforms found stated onboarding preference decays against behaviour. Prefer a cheap explicit re-run over an invisible decay model.
limitations: Costs client time.

name: Revealed-preference signal from delivered-work approvals
source: Hinge infers rankings from like/pass; Stitch Fix updates in real time
claim: Client approvals/rejections of delivered designs are the highest-quality preference signal available and cost nothing to collect.
limitations: Slow, sparse, and confounded with non-aesthetic factors (deadline, budget).

name: Regulated industries constrain the stimulus space a priori
source: b2b-template-shelf-report.md: healthcare PHI, law firm privilege, insurance document authority
claim: Healthcare, legal, insurance, mortgage clients should not be shown high-chroma, high-motion, low-contrast packs at all — prune before eliciting.
limitations: Risks the pruning being wrong and the client wanting distinctiveness.

name: Accessibility floor is not a preference axis
claim: Contrast below AA is never offered regardless of stated preference. The client cannot choose to fail WCAG.
limitations: Removes a genuine aesthetic direction (low-contrast minimalism).

name: End-user vs operator preference divergence
source: b2b-template-shelf-report.md: property_management tenant portal is 'a distinct untrusted identity'; it_services_msps 'per-client tenancy is the product'
claim: For the 6/17 industries where `portal` is secondary, the person choosing (the operator) is not the person using (the end customer). Elicit from the operator but weight toward end-user norms.
limitations: No mechanism yet for representing the absent end user.

name: Density preference conditioned on archetype
source: b2b-template-shelf: case_workflow primary for 6/17, portal secondary for 6/17
claim: Two archetypes carry the majority of catalogue demand; density expectations differ sharply between a dense case-workflow console and a sparse client portal.
limitations: Adds a conditioning variable.
disposition: ADOPT — cheapest useful form of I78

name: Conservative-industry prior on chroma and motion
source: accounting_firms, law_firms, insurance_agencies, mortgage_brokers variant deltas
claim: Seed these industries from a low-chroma, low-motion region of knob space.
limitations: Stereotyping risk; must be a prior the client can override in 2-3 rounds.

name: Expressive-industry prior
claim: Seed from a higher-chroma, higher-expressiveness region.
limitations: Same stereotyping risk.

name: Industry prior must be overridable within 3 rounds
claim: Guarantee the prior is a starting point, not a cage: a client must be able to move out of their industry's region quickly.
limitations: Requires measuring prior strength.

name: Bespoke motion and illustration explicitly out of scope
claim: The spec bottleneck loses hand-tuned parallax and custom artwork. Do not let a knob imply a capability that does not exist.
limitations: Removes a real source of client delight.

name: The preference learner must itself be A/B tested against a static default
source: Spotify Engineering: a bandit is 'a feature you've built, not an experimental method'
claim: Without a holdout comparing elicited packs to an industry-default pack, we cannot claim the elicitation works at all.
limitations: Needs enough clients for a powered comparison — likely the binding constraint.
disposition: ADOPT — the single most important methodological gate

name: Measure the knob-correlation matrix before assuming low effective dimension
source: derived §4; Jamieson & Nowak's d log n is contingent on the embedding assumption holding
claim: The whole few-rounds argument rests on effective d < 7. Measure it, do not assume it.

name: Do not cite Miller 7+/-2 to justify gallery size
source: Miller 1956 is about absolute judgment and memory span, not interface option counts
claim: Citing it would not survive a technical client's scrutiny.

name: Do not cite the jam study as a design principle
source: Scheibehenne et al. 2010: D = 0.02, CI95 [-0.09, 0.12], 63 conditions, N = 5,036
claim: Choice overload does not robustly replicate; size galleries on information grounds.

name: Do not promise a specific accuracy number before measuring
source: ui-pick-to-spec §4.2 no-figure-found; the 728-vs-113 connector error class
claim: No published benchmark measures our task; any quoted figure would be extrapolation.

name: Treat the live demo's convergence claims as unmeasured
source: actionist-taste.pages.dev asserts '~10 picks instead of ~50' with no measurement
claim: Our own prototype's marketing claims must not be recycled as evidence into a client deliverable.

name: Continuous preference vector internally, closed pack at the boundary
source: derived §8; token-pack-science gates A-J; lane synthesis 'learn a vector not a pack ID'
claim: Catalogue can grow without re-eliciting; shipped artefact is always gate-passing.
limitations: Nearest-neighbour metric weighting is an open parameter.
rationale: Resolves the central architectural question (d): continuous vector internally, closed gate-passing pack at the boundary. Everything downstream — catalogue growth, accessibility guarantees, overfitting control — depends on this split being right.

name: The preference learner must itself be A/B tested against a static default
source: Spotify Engineering: a bandit is 'a feature you've built, not an experimental method'
claim: Without a holdout comparing elicited packs to an industry-default pack, we cannot claim the elicitation works at all.
limitations: Needs enough clients for a powered comparison — likely the binding constraint.
disposition: ADOPT — the single most important methodological gate
rationale: Without a holdout against a static industry-default pack we cannot claim the learner works at all. Spotify's framing is decisive: a personalisation system is a feature, not an experimental method. This is the gate that turns the lane from plausible into measured.

name: Warm-start prior from a population aesthetic model
source: LAION aesthetic predictor; Brochu et al. 2010 cut iterations 11.25 -> 6.5 with a learned prior
claim: Learn the client's DEVIATION from a population baseline rather than their taste from scratch. The largest single efficiency lever reported anywhere in the applied literature.
limitations: Population aesthetic is not per-client taste and may encode a generic bias.
rationale: A warm-start population prior is the largest single efficiency lever reported anywhere in the applied literature: Brochu et al. 2010 cut iterations from 11.25 to 6.5. It is also cheap, since the LAION aesthetic predictor already exists.

name: Perturbation-tolerance test
claim: Show the converged pack and a +/-1-level perturbation. If clients reliably distinguish and reject, the tolerance argument in §2 collapses and round counts triple.
rationale: The perturbation-tolerance test is falsifier F1 and should run FIRST, because the entire round-count argument rests on +/-1-level tolerance being acceptable. If it is not, the requirement roughly triples and the product changes shape.

name: Brand-constraint hard cutoffs before elicitation
claim: Existing brand colours/fonts become hard prunes of the stimulus space, not soft preferences; all later stimuli satisfy them.
limitations: Over-pruning can empty the space; needs a fallback.
rationale: Sawtooth's must-have/unacceptable cutoff mechanism is the missing piece for brand constraints, and it is proven commercial practice. A hard prune is categorically better than learning a client's non-negotiables as a soft preference.

name: Simulate-to-size: Monte Carlo power analysis for round count
claim: Answer 'how many rounds' EMPIRICALLY by simulating synthetic clients under a BT likelihood rather than arguing from bounds.
limitations: Power analysis is built for GLM responses; needs adapting.
disposition: ADOPT — this is how the N question should actually be settled
rationale: Simulate-to-size settles the 'how many choices' question empirically rather than by argument. Given that no paper gives a sufficiency guarantee for our setting, a Monte Carlo power analysis over synthetic clients is the only route to a defensible number.

name: Two-week test-retest stability as the primary validation metric
claim: A model that fits the clicks but changes answer next Tuesday is worthless. Measures whether the thing we claim to measure exists.
limitations: Requires client time two weeks apart; hard to get.
rationale: Two-week test-retest is falsifier F7 — the one that would kill the part rather than adjust it. If preference is not stable, no amount of elicitation precision matters. Test early and cheaply.

name: P05 corpus components as re-themable controlled stimuli
source: research/21st-corpus-audit-2026-08-27.md — 86.7% of colour-bearing CSS rules already resolve through var(--token); 87.3% carry a shadcn oklch :root block
claim: Use the 8,515-identity corpus as the stimulus pool: identical structure, varying token pack, re-theming is a find-and-replace on ~30 custom properties.
limitations: 271 components lack previews; component SOURCE is absent from the corpus.
rationale: The P05 corpus turns stimulus generation from a cost into an asset: 8,515 identities, 86.7% of colour rules already indirected through tokens, re-theming as a ~30-property find-and-replace. Identical structure with varying treatment is the ideal experimental article.

name: 4-up gallery with explicit outside option
source: derived §3 + Sawtooth 4-5 per screen + live demo
claim: 2.32 noiseless bits/round; ~0.91 effective at p=0.15; balances information against deliberation cost and avoids the hostility of 'worst'.
limitations: Best-worst is strictly more informative per question.
rationale: The primary format recommendation — 4-up with an explicit outside option — supported independently by the information derivation, Sawtooth's 4-5-per-screen guidance, and our own working prototype.

name: End-user vs operator preference divergence
source: b2b-template-shelf-report.md: property_management tenant portal is 'a distinct untrusted identity'; it_services_msps 'per-client tenancy is the product'
claim: For the 6/17 industries where `portal` is secondary, the person choosing (the operator) is not the person using (the end customer). Elicit from the operator but weight toward end-user norms.
limitations: No mechanism yet for representing the absent end user.
rationale: The operator-vs-end-user divergence is a genuine unsolved design problem that affects 6 of 17 industries, and nobody in the commercial denominator has solved it. Naming it now prevents shipping a system that optimises for the wrong person.
